A1.justification: The authors, neural-curvature construction, proposition, and overlapping experiments identify the same research despite the title change. Both PDFs are readable, but v1 ends with references on page 21 despite referring to appendices. Earlier supplementary details therefore cannot be fully compared with v2's Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original pruning experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, together with component, calibration-size, weight-decay, and per-layer analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original pruning results and reports additional baseline comparisons, aggregation and seed experiments, and runtime and memory measurements.

M1.justification: The core inverse-weight graph, activation-dependent curvature, and minimum-based parameter ranking are retained. Section 7 adds an evaluated hybrid variant that first performs magnitude pruning to an accuracy-loss threshold and then applies curvature pruning to the remaining parameters.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate image classification on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. Additional training configurations and sensitivity experiments retain these datasets and task requirements.

E2.justification: v1 compares against magnitude pruning, SNIP, and SynFlow. v2 adds the post-training Hessian-based SparseGPT baseline to the benchmark and weight-decay comparisons, including the Tanh plots whose legends show its participation. SynFlow is removed from the Tanh comparisons, substantially revising the comparator set across existing experiments.

E3.justification: The stated calibration sizes and pruning without retraining are retained. v2 expands CIFAR-100 evaluation from one ReLU model to three configurations, explicitly covering two CE learning rates and WD. New protocols compare aggregation rules, test SynFlow with 5, 50, and 100 iterations, measure computational resources, and evaluate hybrid pre-pruning with an accuracy-loss threshold of 0.025.

E4.justification: v2 adds minimum/mean/maximum ranking ablation (Figure 5b), calibration-selection and model-initialization sensitivity (Figure 8), hybrid scalability analysis (Figure 9), and SynFlow iteration sensitivity (Appendix A.10). Existing component, calibration-size, weight-decay, and per-layer analyses are retained or relocated. Additional appendix panels supply evidence that v1 sometimes mentions without including.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. v2 Section 6.3.5 tests three calibration sets and three model initializations, reporting mean pruning curves with minimum-to-maximum envelopes across the three models. This introduces an explicit uncertainty-reporting practice, although its coverage is limited to the CIFAR-10 CE ReLU setting.

E6.justification: v2 adds SparseGPT results, an expanded CIFAR-100 configuration comparison, aggregation and seed findings, and computational measurements; it removes Tanh SynFlow curves. New findings favor minimum aggregation and report improved SynFlow performance with five iterations. Within v2, Table 1 reports 1060.574 seconds per example for curvature versus 675.012 for the hybrid, with peak memory increasing from 13493.0 to 17201.2 MB.

T1.justification: The background probability definition changes from proportional weighting in v1 Definition 3 to explicit exponential normalization in v2 Definitions 2 and 4. Section 5.5 also corrects v1's self-referential shortest-path recurrence with a layer-recursive min-plus expression. Proposition 1 and its proof are retained, with the proof moved to Appendix A.6 and its probability distributions explained more explicitly.

C1.justification: v1 explicitly distinguishes its information-flow analysis objective from reducing network size and uses pruning primarily for evaluation. v2 makes post-training pruning the central problem and contribution throughout the title, abstract, introduction, problem statement, and conclusion. It also explicitly limits the evaluated models to small-to-medium sizes and introduces a claim about hybrid scalability.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking SparseGPT's uneven performance to convolutional spatial coupling and training objectives, interprets the seed experiments as evidence of stability, and questions the suitability of the standard SynFlow iteration budget. Its expanded discussion addresses measured computational costs and hybrid mitigation. It also explains that CIFAR-100 adversarially trained models were excluded because of substantial accuracy loss.

D1.justification: v1 refers to training details in an appendix absent from the supplied PDF. v2 Appendices A.2-A.4 provide optimizer, learning-rate, weight-decay, PGD, normalization, and layer-level architecture details. v2 also adds a project code URL, a SparseGPT implementation pointer, and runtime/memory information. These improve documented reproducibility without establishing that previously unspecified settings changed.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused around pruning at initialization versus post-training pruning, adding SparseGPT, Kumar et al.'s information-theoretic pruning barriers, and Wang et al.'s gradient-flow pruning work. The earlier robustness/OOD motivation and several information-flow and learning-based pruning references are removed. This accompanies a substantive repositioning as a graph-based post-training pruning approach.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around pruning. Implementation becomes Section 5.5; Algorithm 1 and the proof move to Appendices A.5-A.6; Tanh comparisons and per-layer discussion move into organized appendix sections. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The original combined benchmark Figure 3 is reorganized into a ReLU comparison and appendix Tanh Figure 10, with revised legends and comparator curves. Per-layer and Tanh weight-decay displays move to the appendix. v2 adds aggregation, seed-variation, hybrid, and iteration-sensitivity plots, additional supplementary panels, and the runtime/memory Table 1.

improvement.justification: Relative to the supplied v1, v2 substantially strengthens assessability by supplying missing training and architecture details, adding a relevant post-training comparator, testing ranking and baseline-budget choices, reporting variation across runs, and quantifying computational costs. These address important reproducibility and validation gaps. The seed study remains narrow, and the hybrid reduces runtime while increasing peak memory, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.
